summary: Gives the reasoning for moving RIP version 1 to historic status. The main reason is its classful nature, meaning it carries no subnet mask information. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC explains why RIPv1 was declared historic: it does not carry subnet masks and is difficult to use with variable-length subnetting and supernetting. It recommends RIPv2 where a RIP protocol is needed.

questions: why can't ripv1 handle variable-length subnetting
what does rfc 1923 recommend instead of ripv1
subtitle: Why RIPv1 was declared historic for use on the global Internet.

tldr.problem: RIPv1's classful routing behavior could not handle subnet masks, variable-length subnetting, or supernetting reliably on the changing Internet.
tldr.mechanism: The memo explains that RIPv1 packets carry no prefix masks and that its distance-vector behavior is limited by a maximum of 16 hops.
tldr.outcome: The applicability statement recommends RIPv2 when RIP is needed and limits RIPv1 to simple topologies where its capabilities suffice.

today: RFC 1923 is an Informational applicability statement explaining why RIPv1 was declared Historic for global Internet use. It recommends RIPv2 for networks that need RIP.

sections.title: RIPv1's Changing Applicability
sections.content: RIPv1 was an early dynamic routing protocol for sharing network reachability in relatively simple topologies. The RFC says the Internet changed with the introduction and use of subnets and CIDR, and RIPv1 could no longer be considered applicable for the global Internet.
sections.plainLanguage: RIPv1 was designed for simpler networks. Later use of subnets and CIDR exposed limits that made it unsuitable for global Internet routing.

sections.title: Classful Addresses and Missing Masks
sections.content:
RIPv1 packets do not carry prefix masks. For non-local addresses, the prefix length is inferred from the address's natural classful length; for networks with a local interface, RIPv1 assumes the local mask applies to all subnets of that network.

As a result, the memo says RIPv1 cannot be used with variable-length subnetting and is difficult to use with supernetting. Exchanging routes with more advanced protocols can also be problematic because mask information may be lost.
sections.plainLanguage: RIPv1 does not send the mask that says how much of an address is the network prefix. It guesses from the address class, which causes problems when subnet sizes differ.

sections.title: Distance-Vector Hop Limit
sections.content: RIPv1 is a simple distance-vector protocol. It uses techniques such as Split Horizon and Poison Reverse, but can still need to count to infinity to remove bad routes, delaying convergence. The memo defines infinity as 16 hops, so networks with a diameter larger than that cannot use RIP.
sections.plainLanguage: RIPv1 can take time to remove a bad route. It also treats 16 hops as infinity, so it cannot serve networks larger than that limit.

sections.title: Recommendation and Historic Status
sections.content:
The applicability statement says RIPv1 has been declared Historic. It recommends RIPv2 for networks that have reason to run RIP, while allowing RIPv1 in simple topologies with fixed subnetting, a default route for external traffic, or no connection to other organizations.

The memo notes that RIPv1 includes no security functions and recommends RIPv2 for sites concerned about routing security.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC recommends RIPv2 when a network needs RIP. It says RIPv1 is limited to simple cases and has no security functions.
